register: wave-9 authoring register (S-B9 tranche) — part 1 of 2

items.stem: State the general formula of the alkanes in terms of n.
items.modelAnswer: The alkanes follow CnH2n+2, where n is any whole number.

items.stem: Which type of bond runs between the carbon atoms throughout an alkane molecule?
items.modelAnswer: Only single bonds join the carbon atoms in an alkane, which is what makes the family saturated.

items.stem: Explain why an alkane cannot take part in an addition reaction.
items.modelAnswer: Addition needs a C=C double bond that can open, and an alkane's carbons are joined by single bonds only, so there is no double bond for atoms to add across.

items.stem: A molecule of an alkane is found to contain 12 carbon atoms. Deduce its molecular formula.
items.modelAnswer: Substituting n = 12 into CnH2n+2 gives C12H26.

items.stem: Name the alkane whose molecules contain three carbon atoms, and give its molecular formula.
items.modelAnswer: The three-carbon alkane is propane, C3H8.

items.stem: How many bonds surround each carbon atom in a displayed formula of any alkane?
items.modelAnswer: Every carbon is drawn with four single bonds in a displayed formula.

items.stem: Explain what changes from one named alkane to the next in the series from methane to pentane.
items.modelAnswer: The carbon chain grows one atom at a time: each member extends the chain by a further carbon, adding a CH2 step from methane through to pentane.

items.stem: A student draws a displayed formula for ethane but joins the two carbon atoms with a double line. Name the hydrocarbon family the drawing now suggests.
items.modelAnswer: A C=C double bond is the functional group of the alkenes, so drawn that way the picture reads as ethene rather than ethane.

items.stem: Name the two oxides that form from air inside a vehicle engine.
items.modelAnswer: Nitric oxide, NO, and nitrogen dioxide, NO2, are the two engine-formed oxides of nitrogen.

items.stem: Write the balanced equation for the burning of the sulfur impurity in a fuel.
items.modelAnswer: The impurity burns as S + O2 -> SO2.

items.stem: Explain why a catalytic converter is fitted to a car even though nitrogen and oxygen only combine at the high temperatures inside the engine.
items.modelAnswer: Because the exhaust still carries carbon monoxide and unburned hydrocarbons as well as the NOx formed at engine temperature, and the converter renders those harmful gases harmless before they leave the tailpipe.

items.stem: In a blast furnace, air is blown through white-hot coke. State which pollutant gases this process shares with the internal combustion engine.
items.modelAnswer: The same oxides of nitrogen: at such high temperatures air nitrogen reacts with oxygen to give NO and NO2, just as in an engine.

items.stem: Give the balanced equation for the route from sulfur dioxide to the acid it forms in raindrops.
Which two acids form when nitrogen dioxide dissolves in rain water?
items.modelAnswer: A mixture of nitrous acid, HNO2, and nitric acid, HNO3.

items.stem: Explain why carbonate statues in cities suffer more than granite ones from the pollution this note describes.
items.modelAnswer: Acid rain corrodes carbonate rock because the acid reacts with the carbonate in the statue's surface and dissolves it away, while granite offers no carbonate for the droplets to attack.

items.stem: Lightning accompanies a thunderstorm over countryside far from any traffic. Explain which acid-rain precursor can still be forming.
items.modelAnswer: Lightning provides energy for nitrogen and oxygen in the air to combine, so nitrogen oxides still form; the NO2 then reacts with rain water to give nitrous and nitric acids.

items.stem: Give the product of the reaction between ethene and bromine.
items.modelAnswer: The double bond opens and bromine adds across it to give dibromoethane, with one bromine atom on each of the two carbons.

items.stem: State the type of reaction by which alkenes take atoms onto their double bond.
items.modelAnswer: Alkenes undergo addition reactions, with atoms adding across the C=C double bond.

items.stem: Explain why the addition of bromine to an alkene leaves exactly one organic product.
items.modelAnswer: Both bromine atoms join the molecule, one bonding to each of the two carbons of the old double bond, so a single dibromoalkane molecule is the only product.

items.stem: Chlorine is bubbled into liquid propene instead of bromine. Name the organic product formed.
items.modelAnswer: The halogen adds across the C=C in the same way, giving dichloropropane with one chlorine on each double-bond carbon.

items.stem: State the safety reason that makes bromine water the reagent of choice when testing for a C=C bond.
items.modelAnswer: Bromine water is an orange solution that is safer to handle than bromine itself.

items.stem: A few drops of bromine water are added to hexane and the tube is shaken. State the final colour of the mixture.
items.modelAnswer: It stays orange, because the alkane offers no C=C bond for the bromine to add across.

items.stem: Explain, in terms of the bromine present, why the orange colour fades when an alkene is shaken with bromine water.
items.modelAnswer: The bromine atoms bond to the two carbons of the double bond, so no free bromine remains dissolved in the water and the orange colour disappears.

items.stem: Two unlabelled bottles hold hexane and hexene. Describe how one shake-test with bromine water tells them apart.
items.modelAnswer: Shake a little bromine water with each: the alkane leaves the mixture orange, while the alkene decolourises it as bromine adds across its C=C, so the tube that fades identifies hexene.

items.stem: Name the two fraction feedstocks most often cracked in this process.
items.modelAnswer: Kerosene and diesel oil are the usual feedstocks for cracking.

items.stem: Give the approximate temperature, in degrees Celsius, to which hydrocarbons are heated for catalytic cracking.
items.modelAnswer: Around 600 to 700 degrees Celsius, hot enough to vaporise the hydrocarbons.

items.stem: Explain how the alumina or silica used in catalytic cracking helps long-chain molecules fall apart.
items.modelAnswer: The vaporised hydrocarbons pass over the hot powdered alumina or silica, whose surface breaks the covalent bonds, so thermal decomposition follows and the chains split.

items.stem: Cracking a long alkane yields ethene among the products. Explain why the products always include members of two different hydrocarbon families.
items.modelAnswer: The random bond-breaking is a thermal decomposition that delivers a mixture of shorter alkanes and alkenes, so both families appear every time.

items.stem: State what the word supply means when balancing the fractions from crude oil.
items.modelAnswer: Supply is how much of a fraction refining the crude oil can produce.

items.stem: Name the two surplus fractions that are commonly cracked.
items.modelAnswer: Fuel oil and bitumen sit in surplus, so they are the fractions cracked into the wanted shorter-chain products.

items.stem: Explain why an oil refinery cannot simply sell its fractions in the proportions the column delivers.
items.modelAnswer: Because what refining supplies does not match what customers demand: long-chain fractions pile up in surplus while short-chain fuels such as petrol, kerosene and diesel are wanted in larger amounts, so cracking must convert the excess.

items.stem: A refinery finds its fuel-oil tank overflowing while petrol orders go unmet. State the process the refinery should run and the products it should expect.
items.modelAnswer: Crack the surplus fuel oil: heating the vapours to 600-700 degrees Celsius over the hot catalyst gives shorter alkanes and alkenes, easing the petrol shortfall.

items.stem: Write down the general formula that every alkene obeys.
items.modelAnswer: The alkenes follow CnH2n, two hydrogens fewer than the alkane recipe.

items.stem: Which bond defines the functional group shared by all alkenes?
items.modelAnswer: Every alkene carries a C=C double bond as its functional group.

items.stem: Explain why an alkene reacts far more readily than an alkane with bromine.
items.modelAnswer: The C=C double bond can open, letting each carbon form one more single bond with the incoming atoms, whereas an alkane's bonds are already saturated and cannot open, so the alkene is much more reactive.

items.stem: An alkene molecule is measured to contain 6 carbon atoms. Deduce its molecular formula.
items.modelAnswer: Substituting n = 6 into CnH2n gives C6H12.

items.stem: Give the molecular formula of but-1-ene.
items.modelAnswer: But-1-ene is C4H8.

items.stem: Between which two carbon atoms does the double bond sit in pent-2-ene?
items.modelAnswer: Between the second and third carbon atoms of the chain.

items.stem: Explain why every alkene contains two fewer hydrogen atoms than the alkane with the same number of carbons.
items.modelAnswer: Two of the links a saturated chain would spend on hydrogens are taken up by the carbon-carbon double bond, so the family carries two fewer hydrogens: CnH2n instead of CnH2n+2.

items.stem: A student draws but-1-ene with the C=C shown as a single line between the first two carbons. State which family the drawing now represents and what the correct drawing must show.
items.modelAnswer: Drawn with one line between those carbons the picture reads as the alkane butane; the correct displayed formula must show the double bond as two parallel lines.

items.stem: State the property that decides where a hydrocarbon vapour condenses in a fractionating column.
items.modelAnswer: Its boiling point: molecules of similar chain length have similar boiling points, so each fraction condenses at its own height in the column.

items.stem: Describe the temperature gradient inside a fractionating column.
items.modelAnswer: The column is hot at the bottom and cooler towards the top.

items.stem: Explain why crude oil itself is of little direct use before it is separated.
items.modelAnswer: It is a mixture of many different hydrocarbons, and a jumble of chains has no single set of useful properties until the fractions are separated out.

items.stem: A hydrocarbon's boiling point is 320 degrees Celsius. State where in the fractionating column it will condense, giving the reason.
items.modelAnswer: It condenses low down the column, near the hot bottom, because only down there is the temperature below its boiling point; high-boiling vapours never rise far before condensing.

items.stem: State which fraction fuels jet aircraft.
items.modelAnswer: Kerosene is the fraction that fuels jet aircraft.

items.stem: State how viscosity changes as chain length grows along the fraction ladder.
items.modelAnswer: Viscosity rises: the longer molecules attract one another more, so the liquid flows less easily and feels thicker.

items.stem: Explain why volatility falls from refinery gas at the top of the ladder to bitumen at the bottom.
items.modelAnswer: As the molecules grow larger the attractions between them strengthen, so far less evaporates easily: bigger molecules mean lower volatility, which is why bitumen barely evaporates at all.

items.stem: Refinery gas boils below 25 degrees Celsius and bitumen above 350. A refinery stream boils at 180 degrees Celsius. Name its fraction.
items.modelAnswer: At 180 degrees Celsius the stream sits in the kerosene range, the jet-fuel fraction of the ladder.

items.stem: List three products of crude oil other than fuels.
items.modelAnswer: Polymers, lubricants, solvents, detergents and adhesives are all obtained from crude oil - any three of these.

items.stem: State three kinds of transport that run on oil products.
items.modelAnswer: Cars, trains and aircraft all run on oil products.

items.stem: Explain why carbon can form the huge variety of compounds the petrochemical industry sells.
items.modelAnswer: Carbon bonds strongly and repeatedly to itself, building chains and rings of almost any length, which lets it assemble a huge number of organic compounds for the industry to draw on.

items.stem: A country discovers oil and builds its first petrochemical industry. Explain two different ways this changes what the country can make.
items.modelAnswer: Its separated fractions supply transport fuels for cars, trains and aircraft, and the same oil feeds polymers, solvents, detergents and adhesives, so the industry underpins both transport and manufacturing development.
